To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the bioaccessibility of metal ions from soil is linearly dependent on the water exchange rate constant of the metal ion, which is a function of the metal ion's stability constants and its aqueous solubility.

the median bioaccessible concentrations of 23 metals in 19 soil samples ranged between <1% and 41% in the stomach and <1% and up to 63% in the duodenum, and that bioaccessibility is linearly related (R > 0.89) to the water exchange rate of metal cations.
the bioaccessibility of metal ions in soil is linear to the water exchange rate constant of the metal ions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an in vitro method that may predict metal bioavailability in soil.
the development of a mechanistic model that can be used to estimate bioaccessible concentrations of metals in soil and to identify soil properties that may influence bioaccessibility.
understanding the relationship between soil properties and the bioaccessibility of metals under gastrointestinal conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
metal cations with a higher k(H₂O) are more bioaccessible than those with lower k(H₂O).
the bioaccessibility of metal ions in soil is linear with its water exchange rate.
the metal bioaccessibility is linearly related with the k(H₂O).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

bioaccessibility and bioavailability are not necessarily synonymous and that the relationship between bioaccessibility of metals in soils and their desorption rate constant (k(H₂0)) is a useful tool for estimating the bioavailability of metals in soils.
bioaccessibility is not a simple function of metal solubility but instead a complex function of metal solute chemistry and soil properties.
the water exchange rate constant of a metal cation in a soil is linearly correlated with its bioaccessibility in the gastrointestinal tract.
The main takeaway from our work is that
bioaccessibility is a kinetic process, and the rate of metal desorption from soil is a major determinant of the bioaccessibility of metal in soil.
the bioaccessibility of metals is a dynamic process that is influenced by both equilibrium solubility (e.g., pH, redox, complexation) and kinetics (i.e., k(H₂O)).
bioaccessibility is a function of desorption kinetics and not the equilibrium solubility of metal cations.
